Ws in the Chat
DUB-ul-yooz in the CHAT
interjection / phrase (Gen Alpha slang)
From live-stream chat culture of the late 2010s and 2020s, where viewers spam the letter W (for "win") to celebrate a streamer’s success and L (for "loss") to mock a failure. "Drop a W in the chat" or "Ws in the chat" became a streamer’s call for applause, and Gen Alpha uses it out loud at school and home to cheer for someone: a friend’s good grade, a sister’s goal, a dad’s pancake flip.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

"Ws in the chat!" means "Everybody cheer!" — it is the Gen Alpha way of saying "Give it up for him!" It comes from live-stream chats where people type W for "win." The Christian observation: this is one of the redeemable words, because it is a call to celebrate someone else. Scripture commands exactly that: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice" (Rom 12:15). The church is meant to be a room full of Ws for one another: "Wherefore comfort yourselves together, and edify one another" (1Th 5:11); "exhort one another daily, while it is called To day" (Heb 3:13). Good words are a gift: "Pleasant words are as an honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones" (Pro 16:24). The phrase’s twin, "Ls in the chat," is the opposite — a pile-on of mockery — and that is the one to leave behind. A father can tell a five-year-old: "When your brother does something good, we put Ws in the chat — we cheer for him! God loves it when we’re happy for each other." A family that hands out Ws at dinner is practicing 1 Thessalonians 5:11 without knowing it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Live-stream chat call to cheer ("drop a W") carried into Gen Alpha speech — a redeemable habit of rejoicing with them that rejoice, opposite its twin "Ls in the chat."

Ws IN THE CHAT, interj. / phr. (streaming slang, late 2010s–present; Gen Alpha) A call to celebrate someone’s success. "She got first place — Ws in the chat!"

Variants: drop a W, big W, W rizz. Opposite: Ls in the chat (mockery).

From viewers spamming W (win) and L (loss) in live-stream chats.

Decode for parents: one of the kind ones — encourage it, and watch for its L twin.

Webster 1828, the root — CHAT, v.i. To talk in a familiar manner; to talk without form or ceremony.

Key Scripture

Rom 12:15 — "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep."

1Th 5:11 — "Wherefore comfort yourselves together, and edify one another, even as also ye do."

Heb 3:13 — "But exhort one another daily , while it is called To day; lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin."

Pro 16:24 — "Pleasant words are as an honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones."

Modern Corruption

"Ws in the chat" is a call to celebrate another, which Scripture commands; its only corruption is its twin, the pile-on of Ls.

expand to see more

Little to correct here. The habit of public cheering is good, and the phrase invites children to notice and praise one another. The caution is the mirror phrase — "Ls in the chat" — in which a crowd piles mockery on someone who failed. Both come from the same chat culture, and children use both.

Keep the W, drop the L. Make cheering for siblings a household custom. Rejoice with them that rejoice; edify one another; let pleasant words be honeycomb. A boy who learns to type W for his brother is learning to love his brother’s good.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Live-stream chat: W (win) / L (loss) spam (late 2010s) → "drop a W," "Ws in the chat" → Gen Alpha spoken cheer.
